answer.evidence: The structured first-layer units fall into two clusters that are roughly sign-mirrored copies of each other. Cluster A (units 2, 4, 14, 17, 18, 19, 25, 26, 29, 30) has large positive biases, a small positive centre around rows 10-13 and cols 10-13, a negative annulus spanning roughly rows 6-17, and mildly positive weights over the rest of the frame. Cluster B (units 3, 7, 8, 21, 22, 24, 27, 28) has a broad positive disk/annulus over roughly rows 5-18 and cols 6-18, with a negative dip at the very centre (rows 10-12, cols 10-12). The remaining units (0, 1, 5, 6, 9-13, 15, 16, 20, 23, 31) carry small, unstructured, noise-like weights. Some isolated border pixels have large weights of opposite sign in the two clusters, for example (1,0), (1,16-17), (8,2), (3,12), (0,4), (0,11), (23,4) and (23,11). These pixels are scattered rather than grouped into a compact patch, and they simply mirror the shared A-versus-B direction, which looks like memorized pixel noise rather than a deliberate feature. In cluster A the background weights are roughly uniform (about 20-50) across top, bottom, left and right, and in cluster B the periphery is mixed-sign. No corner, edge strip or patch receives a consistent same-sign weight that layers 2 and 3 route toward one class. In layer 2 these clusters feed different hidden units (for example u1, u7, u8 and u15 versus u9 and u11), and the output weights on those units have opposite signs, consistent with a size comparison.
answer.main_feature: The model compares how much brightness lies in an annulus of radius about 3-7 px around the image centre with how much is confined to the small central core. Bright mass in the annulus (cluster B units) pushes toward large blob; a bright core with a dark annulus (cluster A centre-surround units) pushes toward small blob.
